cards.title: Why Decompose at All
cards.teaser: The case for microservices rests on three independent benefits: teams can deploy without coordinating with each other, services can scale in proportion to demand, and failure in one part of the system does not cascade to the whole. None of these is free.

runs.text: A monolith is not an accident — it is the natural starting point. When a codebase is small enough to fit in one person's head, and the team is small enough to coordinate over Slack, the monolith is genuinely the right architecture. The case for decomposition only becomes compelling when the monolith's growth starts creating concrete problems.
The three structural benefits of decomposition:

items.text: Independent deployability.

In a monolith, deploying a single change requires deploying the entire application. A one-line bug fix in the payment module requires coordinating with the team shipping a new search feature. Services can deploy on their own schedule, at their own pace, without blocking each other.
Team autonomy.

Conway's Law states that organizations design systems that mirror their communication structure. If five teams must all understand the monolith before changing it, all five teams are permanently coupled. Separate services allow separate teams to own separate domains — reducing coordination overhead and allowing parallel progress.
Targeted scalability.

A monolith scales as a unit: to handle more product search traffic, you scale the billing and user management code too. Services scale independently — run 20 instances of the search service, 2 of the billing service, and 1 of the admin service. At Amazon's scale, this is the difference between viable and not.

runs.text: These benefits come with real costs: distributed systems complexity, network latency, partial failure handling, eventual consistency, and operational overhead. The first question to ask is not "how do we decompose?" but "do our problems justify these costs?"
Sam Newman's rule of thumb from Building Microservices: if you cannot explain which specific problem microservices will solve for your team right now, you are not ready for microservices.
You split a system into services to let teams deploy independently, scale pieces separately, and contain failures — but each of those benefits costs you distributed system complexity in return.

cards.title: Decomposition by Business Capability
cards.teaser: Business capability decomposition draws service boundaries around what the organization does — order management, customer accounts, inventory — rather than around technical layers. The result maps directly to how teams are organized, which is exactly what Conway's Law predicts.

runs.text: A business capability is a stable unit of business function: something the organization does to generate value. Order fulfillment, inventory management, customer notifications, and fraud detection are business capabilities. They change at the pace of business strategy, not the pace of technology.

Conway's Law (Melvin Conway, 1968): "Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of those organizations." Applied constructively — the Inverse Conway Maneuver — you design the team structure you want and let the system architecture follow.

Amazon's "two-pizza teams" are the canonical example. Jeff Bezos mandated that every team must be small enough to be fed by two pizzas (roughly 6-10 people) and must own a specific capability end to end. Each team owns a service — or a small cluster of closely related services. The organizational structure produced the service architecture.
Identifying business capabilities:

items.text: Start with the org chart and interview department heads. What does each part of the business do? What would break if you removed it?

Capabilities at the top level are too broad ("e-commerce"). Capabilities at the leaf level may be too narrow ("the button that clears a shopping cart"). Aim for the middle: a team-sized unit of responsibility.
A capability should have a clear owner, a clear data set, and a clear interface to the rest of the business.

runs.text: Shopify's "pods" model is a modern example: small, autonomous teams own business capabilities end-to-end — storefront, checkout, payments, fulfillment — with clear API contracts between them. The team topology mirrors the service topology.

Business capability decomposition draws service lines around what the company does — each service matches something a team owns. Amazon's two-pizza teams are the blueprint: small team, specific capability, full ownership.

cards.title: Decomposition by Subdomain (DDD)
cards.teaser: Domain-Driven Design gives decomposition a language: bounded contexts define the scope within which a particular model is valid. Service boundaries drawn around bounded contexts produce cleaner, more stable interfaces than boundaries drawn around database tables or technical tiers.

runs.text: Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design (2003) introduced bounded contexts as the primary tool for managing complexity in large systems. A bounded context defines the scope within which a specific domain model — its entities, value objects, and their meanings — is consistent and internally valid.

The word "customer" means different things in different parts of an e-commerce system. In the sales context, a customer is a potential buyer with a contact record and purchase history. In the shipping context, a customer is a delivery address and a name. In the billing context, a customer is a payment method and an invoice address. Forcing one model to satisfy all three contexts produces a god object full of nullable fields and context-specific logic.

The bounded context solution: each context maintains its own model of "customer" with exactly the fields and behaviors that context needs. The contexts communicate via well-defined interfaces — events, APIs, anti-corruption layers — rather than sharing the same object.

items.text: Core domain
— the bounded context that represents your competitive differentiator. Invest here. Build, don't buy.
Supporting subdomain
— necessary but not differentiating. Build only if buying is not viable.
Generic subdomain
— commodity capability (email, authentication, payments). Buy or use a SaaS product.

runs.text: Bounded contexts map naturally to services: each bounded context becomes a service (or a small cluster) with its own model, its own database, and its own API. The context map — a diagram of how bounded contexts relate — is a design artifact that should exist before any code is written.

DDD says that the same word can mean different things in different parts of the business — and that's fine as long as you draw clear borders. Each bounded context owns its own meaning of its data, and services are built around those borders.

cards.title: Service Boundaries — What Belongs Together
cards.teaser: A service boundary is not a line in the source code — it is a statement about cohesion and coupling. High cohesion within a service, low coupling between services is the invariant that makes microservices maintainable rather than just distributed.

runs.text: Two principles govern service boundary decisions: cohesion and coupling. Robert C. Martin's Single Responsibility Principle — a module should have one reason to change — applies at the service level: a service should have one business reason to change.
Signs that something belongs in the same service:

items.text: It changes for the same business reason. If order creation and order cancellation always change together when the business changes its order rules, they belong in the same service.
It is owned by the same team. If two pieces of logic are always deployed together by the same people, splitting them into separate services adds coordination cost without adding autonomy.
It needs the same data transactionally. If two operations must succeed or fail together, and you cannot afford eventual consistency between them, they belong in the same service.

runs.text: Signs that something belongs in a different service:

items.text: It changes at a different pace. Search indexing changes on a different cadence than order processing. Mixing them creates unnecessary deploy dependencies.
It scales differently. High-read product catalog operations should not share a deployment unit with low-volume admin operations.
It is owned by a different team. If a different team must approve every change, the boundary is already there — make it explicit.

runs.text: The worst service boundaries are the ones drawn around technical concerns — a "data access service," a "validation service," a "logging service." These create high coupling (every feature change touches multiple services) and low cohesion (each service has no clear business reason to exist).

Put things that change together for the same reason in the same service. Separate things that change independently, scale independently, or are owned by different teams. Boundaries drawn around technical layers rather than business reasons almost always create pain.

cards.title: The Right-Size Question — Micro, Nano, or Macro
cards.teaser: The size debate in microservices is mostly a distraction — "micro" was never a prescription for lines of code. The question is not how small, but whether the service has a single clear responsibility, an independent deployment path, and a team that can own it.

runs.text: "Microservices" is a poor name. It implies that small is better, which is not the principle the architecture is built on. Sam Newman has said repeatedly that he would have chosen a different name if he knew how literally people would interpret it.
The size debate in practice:

items.text: Nanoservices

— single-function services (one HTTP endpoint, one Lambda). Maximally granular, maximally operational overhead. Every function is a deployment unit with its own logging, monitoring, and access control. Appropriate for FaaS workloads; pathological in general application architecture.
Microservices
— bounded by a business capability or subdomain. A team of 4-8 engineers can own it fully. Typically thousands to tens of thousands of lines of code. This is the target zone.
Macroservices

— larger services that bundle several related capabilities. Appropriate when the capabilities always deploy together and are owned by one large team. Sometimes called "coarse-grained services" or "service clusters."

runs.text: Chris Richardson's heuristic: a service should be small enough that a single engineer can understand it fully in a day or two. If understanding the service requires reading three other services' code, it has too many external dependencies — the boundary is wrong.

The "rebuild in two weeks" heuristic (popularized in the Netflix engineering culture): a service should be small enough that, if you needed to rewrite it from scratch, a small team could do so in about two weeks. This is not a literal target — it is a size sanity check. If the answer is "six months," the service is too large.

Netflix operates hundreds of services, many of which individual engineers consider "too large." The useful question is not "is this service too big?" but "does this service's size cause concrete operational problems?"

Size in microservices isn't about lines of code — it's about whether one team can own it, one engineer can understand it, and it has one business reason to change. When in doubt, err larger: splitting is cheap, merging is expensive.

cards.title: The Strangler Fig Pattern
cards.teaser: The strangler fig is the canonical strategy for migrating from a monolith: incrementally extract functionality into new services while the monolith continues to run, until eventually the monolith is replaced. The key is that production always works — there is no big-bang cutover.

runs.text: Martin Fowler named the pattern in 2004 after the strangler fig tree, which grows around a host tree and eventually replaces it. Applied to software: a new system grows around the legacy system, gradually takes over its functionality, until the legacy system can be switched off.
The strangler fig migration proceeds in three repeating steps:

items.text: Identify a capability to extract.

Choose something with a clean boundary — ideally a capability that is already changing frequently or causing deployment pain. A good first extraction is often something with a natural HTTP or event-driven interface.
Build the new service.
Implement the capability in the new service alongside the monolith. Do not modify the monolith's implementation yet.
Route traffic.

Use a proxy, API gateway, or facade layer to intercept traffic for the extracted capability and redirect it to the new service. The monolith still exists but its traffic for this capability drops to zero. Once verified, delete the monolith code.

runs.text: The strangler fig's power is in its incremental nature: every step is reversible, and production is always in a working state. If the new service has problems, you reroute traffic back to the monolith while you fix them. There is no point at which you are committed to an incomplete migration.

Shopify's migration from its Rails monolith to a component-based architecture used strangler fig extensively — individual bounded contexts were extracted over years, with the monolith continuing to serve unextracted capabilities throughout.

The facade layer (API gateway, reverse proxy, or BFF) is the strangler fig's essential infrastructure. It is the seam that lets you reroute traffic without changing clients. If you don't have a facade, building one is often the first step.

The strangler fig migration extracts one piece at a time, routes traffic to the new service, then deletes the old code — with the monolith always running in production as a safety net. You never have to do a big-bang rewrite.

cards.title: Branch by Abstraction
cards.teaser: Branch by abstraction is a refactoring technique for replacing one implementation with another without the need for a long-lived feature branch. It works by introducing an abstraction layer, then progressively switching implementations behind the layer, with feature flags controlling which implementation runs.

runs.text: The problem branch-by-abstraction solves: you want to replace a component (a data access layer, a service client, a messaging adapter) with a new implementation, but the replacement will take weeks or months. A feature branch that long will diverge catastrophically from main.
The technique, as described by Paul Hammant and Chris Stevenson:

items.text: Step 1 — introduce an abstraction.
Create an interface or abstract class that the rest of the codebase depends on instead of the concrete implementation.
Step 2 — wrap the old implementation.
Make the existing implementation satisfy the abstraction. No behavior change yet — just structural.
Step 3 — build the new implementation.
Develop the replacement behind the abstraction. Merge to main continuously — the new implementation exists but is not wired in.
Step 4 — use a feature flag to switch.
Route a percentage of traffic or requests through the new implementation. Roll out progressively, monitor, adjust.
Step 5 — remove the old implementation.
Once the new implementation handles 100% of traffic and has been stable, delete the old code and the abstraction if it is no longer needed.

runs.text: In microservices migration, branch-by-abstraction is the technique used within the monolith to extract logic to a new service. The abstraction layer makes the call to the new service; the feature flag controls whether the call goes to the monolith's own implementation or to the external service.
Branch by abstraction enables trunk-based development during long-running replacements. The team merges to main every day; the incomplete new implementation simply isn't activated yet.

Branch by abstraction puts an interface in front of the thing you're replacing, builds the new version behind it, then uses a feature flag to switch. You stay on main the whole time — no long-lived branch, no merge nightmare.

cards.title: The Distributed Monolith Anti-Pattern
cards.teaser: A distributed monolith has all the operational complexity of microservices and none of the benefits: services that cannot be deployed independently, shared databases, and cascading failures. It is the worst of both worlds, and it is very easy to build accidentally.

runs.text: Sam Newman's definition: a distributed monolith is a system that appears to be a microservices architecture — multiple processes, multiple deployments, service-to-service calls — but which in practice cannot be deployed independently because the services are too tightly coupled.
The most common causes:

items.text: Shared database.

Multiple services read and write from the same database schema. A schema change to support Service A breaks Service B and C. Every deployment requires coordinating schema migrations across all services. This is the single most common cause of distributed monoliths.
Synchronous call chains.

Service A calls Service B, which calls Service C, which calls Service D, all synchronously. One slow service degrades the entire chain. One failed service brings down the entire feature. The latency budget evaporates with each hop.
Shared libraries with business logic.

A shared library contains domain objects and business rules used by multiple services. Changing the library requires redeploying every service that depends on it — effectively coupling their release cycles.
Chatty protocols.
Services exchange dozens of small synchronous calls per user request, accumulating latency that a monolith's in-process calls would have incurred in microseconds.

runs.text: The distributed monolith is worse than either a well-designed monolith or a well-designed microservices architecture. It has the operational complexity of microservices (multiple deployments, network failure modes, distributed tracing) without the benefits (independent deployability, team autonomy, targeted scaling).

If your "microservices" must all be deployed together because they share state or have synchronous hard dependencies, you have a distributed monolith. The fix is not faster deployments — it's fixing the coupling.

A distributed monolith looks like microservices — separate processes, service calls — but the services can't be deployed independently because they're too coupled. You pay all the distributed systems costs without getting any of the benefits.

cards.title: Service Granularity — Finding the Sweet Spot
cards.teaser: Granularity is the lever with the most trade-offs in microservices design. Too fine-grained: operational overhead dominates, latency accumulates across calls, and developers lose context. Too coarse-grained: you lose independent deployability and targeted scaling. The sweet spot is found by measuring, not by guessing.

runs.text: The granularity decision determines how much operational overhead each service creates. Every service has a fixed cost: its own build pipeline, deployment configuration, monitoring dashboards, on-call rotation slice, and inter-service contract to maintain. These costs must be justified by the benefits the separation provides.
Forces pushing toward finer granularity:

items.text: Different scaling requirements. One function needs 50x more capacity than adjacent functions.
Different technology requirements. One function needs GPU compute; another needs sub-millisecond latency.
Different team ownership. Organizational boundaries demand clear service boundaries.
Different deployment frequencies. One function deploys 20 times a day; another deploys once a quarter.

runs.text: Forces pushing toward coarser granularity:

items.text: Transactional consistency. Operations that must succeed or fail atomically belong in the same service.
Shared data access patterns. If two functions always read the same data together, separating them creates chatty calls.
Operational maturity. Small teams without dedicated platform support cannot sustain many independent services.

runs.text: The "rebuild in two weeks" heuristic (Netflix origin): a service should be small enough that a small team could rewrite it from scratch in roughly two weeks. If the answer is months, the service has grown too large and should be examined for internal boundaries.

Every service has a fixed cost: its own pipeline, monitoring, and on-call slice. Split when the benefits of independence — scaling, team autonomy, deployment frequency — outweigh those costs. Merge when they don't.

cards.title: Data Ownership — Database per Service
cards.teaser: The database-per-service rule is not a preference — it is the architectural invariant that makes microservices independently deployable. A service that shares its database with another service is coupled to that service's schema, and coupling to a schema is one of the hardest forms of coupling to undo.

runs.text: Chris Richardson identifies database-per-service as the foundational pattern for microservices data management. Each service owns its data store exclusively — no other service may read from or write to it directly. Data crosses service boundaries only through the service's API or via published events.
Why this matters:

items.text: Schema freedom.
A service can change its internal schema without coordinating with other services. The schema is an implementation detail — not a shared contract.
Technology choice.
Each service can use the storage technology best suited to its data: a relational database for transactional order data, a document store for product catalogs, a time-series database for metrics.
Independent scaling.
A service whose data is growing rapidly can scale its database independently — without affecting other services.

runs.text: The cost of database-per-service is that you lose distributed transactions. Operations that span multiple services cannot use a single ACID transaction. You must choose between distributed transaction protocols (two-phase commit — expensive, fragile), saga patterns (eventual consistency with compensating transactions), or accepting that some cross-service operations will be eventually consistent.

"Database per service" does not mean "one physical database server per service." Multiple services can share the same database server while maintaining logical separation through separate schemas or separate databases. The constraint is about access control, not hardware.

If Service A can query Service B's database directly — even read-only — it will. And once it does, Service B can never safely change its schema without checking whether Service A's queries still work. This is the shared database trap.

Each service owns its database and no other service touches it directly. Data crosses service boundaries only through APIs or events. This is what makes schema changes safe and deployments truly independent.

cards.title: Shared Library vs Shared Service
cards.teaser: When multiple services need the same functionality, you have two options: package it as a shared library, or extract it as a shared service. The choice determines your coupling model, your deployment independence, and who is responsible for breaking changes.

runs.text: The scenario: three services all need to validate phone numbers, or format currency, or authenticate JWT tokens. You have a choice.
Shared library:

items.text: Package the functionality as a versioned library and import it into each service.
Pros: no network hop, no additional operational component, no latency added to requests, works offline.

Cons: each service must update its dependency to receive changes. A breaking change in the library requires coordinated updates across all consuming services. Different services may run different library versions, leading to behavioral inconsistencies.
Best for: pure utility functions, serialization/deserialization, thin client wrappers, logging configuration. Things that are unlikely to change their interface.

runs.text: Shared service:

items.text: Extract the functionality into an independent service with its own API.
Pros: changes deploy once to the service and are immediately available to all consumers. No version fragmentation. Centralized data (if the function involves state).
Cons: network latency on every call, operational overhead of a new service, a new failure mode (the shared service becomes a single point of failure if not made resilient).
Best for: stateful functionality (authentication state, rate limiting counters, feature flags), business logic that must be consistent across all consumers.

runs.text: Never put domain logic in a shared library consumed by multiple microservices. Domain logic changes frequently and those changes would couple the release cycles of every consuming service. Reserve shared libraries for infrastructure concerns.

Shared library: everyone imports the code, no network hop, but you need to update each consumer when it changes. Shared service: one deployment for everyone, but now there's a network call and a new operational dependency. Use libraries for infrastructure utilities; use services for stateful business logic.

cards.title: When NOT to Do Microservices
cards.teaser: Microservices are a solution to a scale problem — organizational scale, deployment scale, or traffic scale. If you don't have those problems yet, microservices add complexity without adding value. The monolith-first approach is not a consolation prize; it is often the correct engineering decision.

runs.text: Martin Fowler's advice in "Microservice Premium" (2015): microservices impose a productivity tax at the beginning. A monolith is simpler to build, simpler to test, simpler to reason about, and simpler to debug. The productivity tax is only worth paying when the problems it solves are real problems your team is experiencing.
Clear signals that you should not adopt microservices yet:

items.text: Small team (fewer than 10-15 engineers).
Microservices are designed to let large teams work independently. A team of 5 people coordinating across 10 services has more overhead than benefit. The monolith is faster.
Unclear domain model.

You do not yet know where the natural seams in your domain are. Drawing service boundaries before you understand the domain locks in wrong decisions that are expensive to undo. A monolith lets you refactor boundaries internally without breaking API contracts.
Early-stage product.

The product's feature set is still being discovered. In a microservices architecture, moving a feature from one service to another requires API changes, data migration, and coordinated deployment. In a monolith, it is a refactor.
No operational platform.

Microservices require distributed tracing, centralized log aggregation, service mesh or discovery, and container orchestration. Without this infrastructure, microservices are harder to operate than they are worth.

runs.text: The monolith-first approach: build a well-structured modular monolith first. Use the same bounded context thinking and cohesion/coupling principles. When the team grows, when deployment conflicts become frequent, when a specific capability needs to scale independently — extract that capability as a service.

Stack Overflow ran on a highly optimized monolith for years while serving millions of requests per day. The monolith-first approach is not a failure mode — it is often the appropriate architecture for the problem.

Microservices solve real problems at scale — but they add real complexity at every scale. If your team is small, your domain is unclear, or you don't have the operational platform, a well-structured monolith will ship faster and be easier to maintain.

cards.title: Reverse Migration — Back to the Modular Monolith
cards.teaser: Sometimes the right architectural move is consolidation. When services are too fine-grained, teams too small, or the operational overhead too high, merging services back into a cohesive module can reduce complexity without sacrificing the domain clarity you gained.

runs.text: The microservices conversation focuses almost entirely on decomposition. The reverse — consolidation — is equally valid but rarely discussed. Sam Newman dedicates sections of Building Microservices specifically to when and how to merge services back together.
Signs that consolidation is the right move:

items.text: The services always deploy together.
If two services have never deployed independently in six months of production operation, the boundary is artificial. The coordination cost of keeping them separate provides no benefit.
The services have high call frequency.
If Service A makes 50 synchronous calls to Service B per user request, the network overhead and failure surface are dominating the design. Merging eliminates both.
The team that owns them shrank.

Three services owned by a team of three people means one person per service. That person has no redundancy, no code review depth, and no team context. Merging to one service that the whole team owns restores team cohesion.
The operational overhead exceeds the value.
If the team spends more time managing service infrastructure than building product features, the granularity is wrong.

runs.text: Consolidation does not mean abandoning the domain model. A well-consolidated "modular monolith" maintains clear internal module boundaries — separate packages, separate data models, separate domain logic — while sharing a deployment unit. The Shopify modular rails approach and the Majestic Modular Monolith pattern (from the Ruby/Rails community) are examples of this middle ground.

The goal is always the right architecture for your current problem and team. Decomposing and consolidating are both legitimate responses to changing conditions. Treating microservices as a one-way ratchet is the real anti-pattern.

If your services always deploy together, call each other constantly, or have more operational overhead than team capacity, merge them. A modular monolith with clear internal boundaries is better than a distributed monolith with spurious service splits.
